#3121. Does opting out of TV tracking work?

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿

A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn’t new, but what and how they’re tracking — and if we can stop it — is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was effective for most TVs — including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) — Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart’s Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn’t even happened.

ACR systems sample the audio or video playing on a TV, convert them into digital fingerprints, and send them to a database to identify what’s being watched. TV companies use that information to make recommendations of what to watch next, provide viewing metrics, and allow for targeted ads.

The researchers wanted to understand when ACR was running on each TV, whether opting out did anything, and what type of data ACR systems were capturing. Because there are many different TV operating systems, and manufacturers keep smart TVs locked down, ACR activity needs to be inferred based on where the TV sends data.

Hisense 32A4K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS

Sony KD32W830K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS

To answer those questions, the team developed a suite of automated experiments across all the TV operating systems. They used Northeastern’s Mon(IoT)r software and SPHERE Research Infrastructure testbeds to capture and analyze all network traffic from each TV, which let them determine when ACR tracking was active and figure out where the TVs were likely sending that data.

They played content on each TV from first-party streaming services such as LG Channels and The Roku Channel; third-party streaming like Netflix and YouTube; over an HDMI cable; using the over-the-air antenna; and via screen mirroring, all to see if there was any difference in ACR traffic on different inputs.

They found that several of the TVs tested didn’t seem to have any ACR activity whatsoever, including a Westinghouse Xumo TV and three TVs from Sony, Hisense, and TCL running Google TV OS. (Another Sony TV with Google TV did have ACR enabled.)

Of the TVs with ACR-associated network traffic, all of them scan over-the-air transmissions, while everyone but Google and Amazon uses it on first-party streaming services (such as The Roku Channel and LG Channels).

Third-party apps like Netflix and YouTube? No ACR except a small amount on webOS, which disappears when opted out. Screen mirroring also looks to be safe from monitoring on all TVs but the one running Vidaa OS.

To figure out whether each OS used audio or video fingerprinting, the experimenters played content that had both video and audio, just audio with a black screen, and just video with no audio, and watched for changes in network traffic to the ACR endpoints. They found that Tizen likely uses video fingerprinting, webOS and Vidaa use audio, and Fire TV OS, Google TV OS, Roku OS, and Vizio OS use a combination of both.

Ideally, opting out of ACR activity should stop all data transmission to suspected ACR endpoints, and for webOS, Fire OS, Vidaa OS, and the Sony Google TV, that’s what happened. But it wasn’t always the case. Samsung’s Tizen OS activity decreased, but not completely, with ACR-correlated traffic still showing while using the antenna, first-party streaming, and HDMI. And on the two Roku OS TVs (one from TCL and one from Roku), ACR still applied to the Roku Channel app. TCL discloses this limitation in menu settings, while the Roku TV does not. Opting out on the Vizio TV didn’t change ACR-correlated traffic at all. (Vizio settled a lawsuit with the FTC in 2017 related to consumer data gathering.) I reached out to Walmart for comment about the Vizio TV’s performance in the study but did not hear back before press time.

As the paper notes, because almost all network traffic sent from the TVs to the suspected ACR endpoints was encrypted, the researchers couldn’t be entirely sure that the traffic that remained after opting out was ACR traffic.

“We interpret the continued presence of traffic consistent with ACR tracking after opt-out as suspicious, though we cannot confirm the contents of the network traffic (due to encryption), nor whether data is processed or retained on the server side.”

It doesn’t seem to matter if you opt out during the setup process or later down the line. “For the large-scale automated tests, we applied the opt-out through the TVs’ settings menus after setup, not during the setup process,” project lead professor David Choffnes told The Verge via email. But the researchers “also manually tested certain TVs (the Vizio TV and the Fire TV) after a factory reset, and the results were unchanged,” he told me. The testing order was also randomized to prevent earlier experiments from influencing later ones.

Disturbingly, during the study, the researchers discovered a vulnerability with Vidaa OS exposing unencrypted information. Because of the vulnerability, the researchers were able to access an MQTT broker — an intermediary between Vidaa OS and Unruly, a video ad platform — and receive ACR results from other Vidaa TV users.

“Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can’t be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint.”

Over a period of three hours, they collected data from over 1 million unique TVs. They informed Vidaa of the vulnerability, which the company confirmed and has since addressed by requiring a login for the server (although messages are still sent unencrypted).

The paper recommends ways to protect ourselves from TVs harvesting our data. The easiest is to disconnect your TV from the internet, both wired and wireless, and instead use a streaming device that doesn’t run ACR.

If you want to continue using the built-in apps, they suggest using webOS, Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and Vidaa OS — just make sure to opt out of everything you can. They also provide a blocklist of endpoints you can restrict using blockers like Pi-hole that don’t break the TVs or affect view quality.

I agree that there needs to be more transparency from TV manufacturers about ACR and, more broadly, what data of ours they collect and when. The Northeastern study helps to pinpoint when data is gathered, but there’s still a lot that’s seemingly intentionally hidden. And it shouldn’t be up to independent researchers to discover and disclose any of this. It should be the responsibility of the companies doing the collecting. It’s time for them to stop hiding what they’re doing.

#3120. I Don’t Buy With a Little Help From My Friends

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3119. SpaceX or Micron: If I Could Only Own One for the Next 5 Years, It Would Be This

Between a newly public rocket company with a volatile stock and a concentrated CEO, and a memory chip maker with $100 billion in contracted demand already locked in, here's why one is the easier buy-and-hold pick.

If I were forced to pick only one of these two stocks to own for the next five years, I'd take Micron Technology (MU +2.58%) over SpaceX (SPCX +3.62%), and not because I doubt what SpaceX has built. Rockets that can land themselves safely for reuse and a satellite internet business with real revenue are genuinely remarkable achievements. My hesitation is about the stock and the man behind it, not the rockets.

SpaceX went public in June at $135 per share, first traded at $150, and popped as high as roughly $226 in the days that followed. Then it tumbled to a low of around $105 and has since round-tripped back to around $134 to $140 in recent sessions, close to 40% below its peak.

The bigger issue for me is control. SpaceX's IPO filing spelled out the nature of a dual-class share structure in which Musk's Class B shares carry 10 votes each, while the Class A shares that regular investors can actually buy carry just one vote each. The result: Musk holds around 82% of the voting power while owning less than half the economic stake in the company. As a shareholder, you're along for the ride, not in the driver's seat, and that ride includes a CEO who's also running Tesla (TSLA -1.32%), X, xAI, and a handful of other ventures simultaneously. I don't think that makes SpaceX a bad business. I think it makes it a harder stock to hold for five years, given how tied it will be to wherever Musk's attention goes next.

Micron just closed its best fiscal year ever. Its fiscal 2026 revenue came in at $133.19 billion, up from $37.38 billion the year before, and the fourth quarter alone brought in a record $54.23 billion.  In the company's Sept. 30 earnings release, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra framed it plainly: "AI is becoming Super Intelligence (SI), and memory enhances this intelligence and the competitiveness of our customers' platforms." Micron also guided for roughly $61.5 billion in revenue for its current quarter, which would be another record.

What I find more convincing than the revenue number is how Micron is locking that sales growth in. The company has signed 16 strategic customer agreements -- multiyear take-or-pay contracts with price floors that bind customers to purchase set volumes of memory whether they need it in the moment or not. Management says those agreements carry a cumulative minimum revenue value of roughly $100 billion, and customers have already put up about $22 billion in cash deposits and related financial commitments to back them. That's not Micron hoping demand holds up; that's customers prepaying to guarantee they get supply at all. Micron also pays a dividend of $0.15 per share quarterly, something SpaceX doesn't offer its shareholders in any form.

Both companies are riding real, durable trends; demand for space infrastructure isn't going away, and neither is demand for AI data center memory. But one of these stocks comes with a CEO who controls the board regardless of what public shareholders think and a chart that has already demonstrated how violently it can move, while the other just posted contracted revenue visibility stretching years into the future, backed by customers putting real cash on the table.

Over the next five years, I'd rather own the business with its hand already forced by binding contracts than the one where a single person's attention, mood, or next venture can move the stock overnight. Micron wins that comparison for me, not really because SpaceX is a bad company, but because it's a much harder stock to hold on to.

Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3117. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3115. My Top 5 Stocks to Buy Before 2027 and Hold for a Decade

All of these offer terrific growth opportunities if you buy and hold.

As the market gets closer to ending the year with its fourth consecutive double-digit gain, the S&P 500 is actually down over the past month. There are worries about skyrocketing artificial intelligence (AI) spending, higher interest rates that could slow the economy, and unrelenting inflation that could start giving more consumers pause.

All economies and markets go through cycles, which is why it's so important to have a long-term investing mindset. Trying to time the market can lead to poor timing and losses, while study after study has shown that it's time in, not timing, the market that drives wealth generation.

Here are five stocks with excellent long-term prospects that I believe can lead to fabulous wealth creation if you hold on for the next 10 years.

I debated which large-scale retailer to put on this list, because Costco Wholesale, Walmart, and Target (TGT -2.51%) each offer value for investors. However, the former two stocks are quite expensive right now, which is why Target, trading at a forward P/E ratio of 16, looks like the bargain to buy right now.

Target has been through a lot over the past few years, and it's shown up in lower comparable sales and profits. Target stock is still 42% off its high, but it's made a comeback this year, up 58%.

The market is celebrating the company's wins this year, including a 3.8% increase in comparable sales in the 2026 fiscal second quarter (ended Aug. 1) and earnings per share of $4.11, up from $2.05 last year.

I believe Target can recover and go on to bigger and better things. It's much smaller than Walmart and only U.S.-based, which provides ample expansion opportunities, and it has faced similar challenges before and bounced back. It was way ahead of Costco and Walmart in e-commerce adoption, and it's likely to embrace new technology.

Finally, it's a Dividend King, and it has raised its dividend for the past 54 years, which is passive income you can rely on.

Dutch Bros (BROS -0.66%) is a small coffee shop chain that's expanding quickly. Customers love its exclusive custom beverages that lean toward the cold and the sweet, differentiating it from the standard coffee shop chain. Its portfolio consists predominantly of drive-thru locations, and it's focused on quick, friendly customer service, which matters to today's consumers.

The company consistently demonstrates robust growth, backed up by new stores and increased same-store sales. Total revenue was up 32% year over year in the second quarter, and same-store sales were up 5.8.%. It's also highly profitable, and earnings are rising as the company scales.

Dutch Bros has 1,225 stores as of the end of the second quarter, but it plans to nearly double by 2029. It sees a long-term opportunity of 7,000 stores, and in 10 years it could reach that goal.

MercadoLibre (MELI -0.87%) has a dual ecosystem including the largest e-commerce platform in Latin America and one of the largest and fastest-growing finance apps. It has a major edge in the ecosystem aspect, keeping customers more engaged on the platform.

The company consistently boasts high growth, with a 50% year-over-year sales increase in the second quarter, its highest in nearly four years. There's momentum across the platform, with a 44% increase in gross merchandise volume, a 14% increase in units per buyer (despite a 26% increase in active buyers), and a 56% increase in total payment volume.

Management feels it has many levers to pull to generate higher growth, and it keeps bringing out improvements and new features. It has a membership program called Meli+ that includes streaming subscriptions, and it recently lowered its free shipping threshold in its largest market, Brazil, which has led to accelerating growth there.

MercadoLibre stock was down 19% this year due to falling profits that it says are necessary to invest in future growth, and it looks like a stock to buy on the dip.

e.l.f. Beauty (ELF +0.74%) is a young mass cosmetics and skincare company that has soared to the top of the industry. The brand, which stands for eyes, lips, face, is demonstrating fantastic growth, and it has continued to introduce new products and lines that captivate its core clientele of fun-loving, eco-conscious consumers.

It also recently entered the luxury market with its acquisition of Rhode, a great sign of what the company can do to generate higher growth.

In the 2027 fiscal first quarter (ended June 30), sales increased 36% year over year. e.l.f. is focused on value, and for a long time it priced all of its products at $1. It has since raised prices to offset higher costs, but it's still a magnet for beauty customers as inflation makes it harder to spend money.

The company was battered by higher tariffs last year, but it's since absorbed the impact, and its margins are improving; gross margin was 83% in the first quarter, 14% percentage points higher than last year.

e.l.f. stock is 49% off its high, but it's up 47% year-to-date, and it's a great time to catch it on the way up.

On Holding (ONON +2.76%) is a newcomer to the athletic-wear industry, and it's quickly capturing market share, becoming the shoe of choice for its affluent client base.

The Swiss company has been growing fast despite the challenging economy and expanding its presence across the globe. While competitors like Nike and Lululemon Athletica have struggled, On has reported strong growth and profits.

In the second quarter, sales increased 22% (currency-neutral) year over year and gross margin improved from 61.5% to 65.4%. That's because the company's premium positioning allows it to charge higher prices, and more customers are willing to pay full price.

The market liked its recent investor day update, when management said it expects high-teens growth through 2029 and a gross margin of at least 65%.

On stock is down 27% year-to-date, but at 16 times next year's earnings, now is a good time to buy.

Jennifer Saibil has positions in Dutch Bros, MercadoLibre, On Holding, and Walmart. #3112. To Defend Against AI Attackers, Start Thinking Like One

Yair Grindlinger is CEO and Co-Founder of Surf AI.

AI is not black magic. It still has to work through real systems, identities, applications and infrastructure, which means its limits are knowable. That matters, because fear is only useful when it’s aimed at the right things.

For enterprises, the right thing to fear is how AI changes the attacker. AI-driven attacks are faster, more persistent and more sophisticated, and they can exploit a single critical weakness or chain together a handful of small ones until they find a way in. ​​

There are several obvious ways AI changes attacks. First is speed. We’re seeing attacks happen in hours instead of days or weeks because AI systems can operate 24/7. The window for defenders is already shrinking. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report found that the average time it took criminal attackers to move from initial access deeper into a network​ fell to 29 minutes, and the fastest observed breakout took just 27 seconds.

But I think stamina may be even more important than speed. A typical human attacker might spend a few hours trying to get into an organization. If nothing works, they may move to the next victim. AI doesn’t necessarily have that limitation. If you tell an AI system to find a way in, it can keep working 24/7 until it finds something.

Then there is breadth of knowledge. Human attackers are typically good at something, whether it’s social engineering, zero-days or a particular system. AI can have the whole playbook. The same system can work across identity, software vulnerabilities, configurations and other attack surfaces. Because it has both stamina and breadth of knowledge, it can connect those weaknesses together.

That ability to connect weaknesses changes how we need to think about exposure. An attack might begin with an exposed secret, then move to an asset with a risky configuration, a software vulnerability or an identity problem. Each issue might look relatively insignificant on its own. You might classify each one as medium or low risk and decide none is critical enough to demand immediate attention. But together, they can create a critical attack path.

Microsoft made essentially the same point in its July 2026 “Secure Future Initiative“ progress report, noting that attackers can use “frontier models to discover vulnerabilities, chain attack paths, and scale exploitation faster than manual approaches allow.” It also observed that serious security failures can emerge when identity gaps, unmanaged assets and inconsistent configurations sit next to one another.

The Hugging Face intrusion offers a vivid example. In July 2026, the company disclosed that an autonomous AI agent, which had escaped an AI lab’s evaluation environment, carried out an end-to-end intrusion into part of its production infrastructure, with no human directing its steps. The attack moved from code-execution weaknesses to credential harvesting and lateral movement across internal clusters. Hugging Face later reconstructed roughly 17,600 attacker actions as the system searched for a viable path.​ ​Most of those actions failed. The agent simply kept going until something worked.

A human attacker may look for one big open window and move on if it isn’t there. AI will find that window faster, and if it isn’t there, it will patiently look for the little things and chain them together.

Attackers and defenders often see the environment differently. From a defender’s perspective, we frequently manage security in islands. There may be a cloud vulnerability team, an identity team, IT teams and someone else responsible for third-party applications. The attacker doesn’t care about those organizational boundaries. To the attacker, all of those things are part of the same attack surface.

Suppose a team is looking at a cloud vulnerability. On its own, it might not appear urgent. But what if the asset can be accessed by someone whose MFA is misconfigured and who also uses a highly privileged third-party application? If the teams responsible for those areas don’t know the issues are connected, they don’t understand the real priority.

That becomes especially important as AI gives defenders visibility into more exposures. In many cases, these weaknesses were probably always there. We simply know about more of them now. That’s a good thing because defenders can use powerful tools to find the same types of exposures attackers are looking for.

The problem is that organizations will get a lot of results. It will be impossible to manage everything at once. Prioritization therefore has to change. Instead of looking only at how severe an individual vulnerability appears to be, ask whether it is exposed, how it connects to other weaknesses and whether it forms part of an attack chain.

A critical exposure on an important asset still demands attention, whether or not it’s part of a chain. But something that appears lower-risk may also offer a quick win because fixing it breaks a larger chain.

AI has made finding vulnerabilities faster and easier than ever. Closing them still depends on knowing who owns the affected asset, understanding what a fix could affect and getting approval, and that’s where most organizations get stuck. In many of my conversations with CISOs, we never get to attack chains. They have critical exposures they can’t close.

One CISO at a large enterprise told me that 25% to 35% of employees leave or change roles in a given year. Many of them own systems, and the asset inventories meant to track that are almost never up to date. So security teams spend their days chasing people to find out who can approve a fix. That isn’t the job anyone signed up for, and it’s the bottleneck that keeps exposures open. Before you can think in chains, you have to be able to close the basics quickly.​

I see two fundamental requirements for responding to this shift. First, organizations need to know their assets: what they have, who owns each one and what a change could affect. Second, they need automation operating continuously on top of that knowledge.

If attackers are operating at machine speed, defenders cannot depend entirely on human-speed processes. Organizations need systems that continuously collect information, connect exposures and help security teams identify which problems matter most.​​ Then they need to get each fix to the right people, because a prioritized list nobody can act on doesn’t reduce risk.

This matters even for threats no one has seen yet. You can’t patch a zero-day before you know it exists, but you can shrink your blast radius every day by closing the exposures around it, so the next one matters less before it’s even disclosed. And when it does land, you can be ready to answer “are we exposed?” in hours, not weeks.​

For CISOs, my practical advice is to pause and rethink exposure management. The way we have managed exposure until today isn’t necessarily going to work for the AI era. Assign someone, or create a team, whose job is to think about exposure holistically. Then reconsider the people, process and technology required to support that approach.

AI creates real reasons for concern. But the most useful fear is a specific one: attackers are becoming faster, more persistent and more sophisticated. Defenders need to respond in kind: know their assets, shrink their blast radius every day and be ready for the next one.

In other words, we need to start thinking a little more like the attackers.​

#3111. Gartner: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Retention, not new sales, is what the transformation is built to protect, and it feeds the metric driving top-line growth.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Gartner (IT -13.19%) raised its full-year financial outlook as contract value growth accelerated for the third consecutive quarter. For long-term investors, the company's ability to expand margins while aggressively reducing its share count demonstrates underlying business resilience despite broad economic uncertainty. Three key insights from management stand out for long-term investors.

Enterprise leaders struggle to derive measurable productivity benefits from third-party artificial intelligence, or AI, software. Gartner guides corporate executives through effective strategy implementation, turning widespread technological disruption into expansion opportunities for its core research subscriptions.

Management is maintaining a rigorous share buyback strategy, allocating available free cash flow to repurchase stock when prices are favorable. This ongoing reduction in outstanding shares concentrates future earnings power and boosts long-term returns for remaining shareholders.

Through its Business Transformation Initiatives, the firm is improving the timeliness and analytical impact of its research content. Faster insights directly improve client retention, which boosts net contract value increase, or NCVI, the key metric driving overall top-line growth.

Enterprise spending cycles are showing clear signs of stabilization across core practice areas, and Gartner leverages its vast research footprint, strong pricing discipline, and high client retention to navigate broader budget pressures while sustaining double-digit return on invested capital.

Long-term value creation remains centered on cash generation and disciplined capital allocation. By continually expanding research coverage across emerging technologies, the business maintains a structural competitive moat that reinforces its market leadership.

The Motley Fool recommends Gartner. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3108. If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Says SCHD’s Dividend Grew Through the Last Two Bear Markets. But Here’s the Catch I'm Watching.

SCHD's history is encouraging, but one recent number changes how I read it.

With the market on edge these days, especially heading into Friday's jobs report, a question keeps nagging income investors: What will happen to my dividends if stocks crash?

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD -0.97%) has already endured two bear markets since its inception in 2011. The S&P 500 fell about 34% in early 2020 and again by over 24% in 2022. Yet SCHD's annual dividends per share rose about 49% from 2019 to 2022, from a split-adjusted $0.57 to $0.85 per share.

I own the ETF and added to my position last week, so I wanted to know what that record can -- and can't -- tell us. Here's a recent catch in its dividend record that I'm watching very closely.

Adjusted for the ETF's 2024 3-for-1 share split, the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF paid roughly $0.57 per share in 2019, $0.68 in 2020, $0.75 in 2021, and $0.85 in 2022, according to the distribution history on its website. That's an increase of 17.6% in the year of the COVID crash and 13.9% in the year of the bear market.

However, while the dividend went up both times, SCHD's share price didn't escape the downdraft. Its worst three-month return was -21.6% in early 2020. It also declined during the 2022 bear market.

One caution when you look at the payout history is that SCHD's quarterly payments swing wildly:

So, while the payout grew in both 2020 and 2022, it wasn't a straight line.

SCHD's dividend didn't just grow through those downturns. It grew fast. Overall, dividends per share have grown at a 9% compound annual rate from 2020 through 2025. However, over the past 12 months, the payout has only increased by about 2% compared to the prior year.

That's a sharp slowdown, and it matters because the case for a dividend growth ETF rests on that growth. I don't know yet whether it's a blip or a trend. If the pace stays near 2%, the resilience we saw in 2020 and 2022 is worth less than it looks.

It's also worth noting that no two crashes are the same. For example, the 2020 crash was brutal but brief, and the 2022 decline was driven by rising inflation and interest rates. So, a deeper, longer earnings recession would be a tougher test for the dividend.

The slowdown doesn't erase why SCHD's payout held up in the past. The ETF tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which screens for yield, five-year dividend growth, and financial strength. The index also revamps its holdings once a year, swapping out companies that no longer measure up.

The ETF holds many large companies with long histories of dividend growth. Its top holdings include Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola. Big, established businesses like these tend to have the cash flow and financial strength to keep paying through a downturn. Procter & Gamble has raised its dividend for 70 straight years, while Coca-Cola is up to 64 straight years. They're both Dividend Kings, companies with 50 or more years of annual dividend increases.

If the last two crashes are any indication, SCHD's dividend will likely keep rising while its share price would probably decline during a market slump. Depending on the catalyst, it might decline less than the S&P 500, due to the more defensive nature of its holdings, its strong dividend income, and its current valuation (at 18.2 times earnings, it's cheaper than the S&P 500 at 23.6 times earnings).

That's not a bad combination if you're collecting dividends. SCHD currently has a trailing 12-month yield of more than 3%. If its share price declines while its payout continues to rise, investors could lock in an even higher yield on newly purchased shares, enabling them to generate even more dividend income in the future.

I'm not selling SCHD because a stock market crash could be coming, as the ETF's history gives me some comfort. It has historically continued paying a higher dividend, even though its share price has taken a hit. However, the catch is that dividend growth has significantly slowed more recently despite a solid economic environment. That's why I'll be watching its next payout announcement in December to see if the slowdown is just a temporary blip or something more concerning.

Matt DiLallo has positions in Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble, and Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF. The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.57% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3103. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3101. Apollo Global: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Apollo is keeping its own debt-like returns and avoiding equity-style risk in AI deals, a discipline that matters if the private credit push slows.

On its third-quarter earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Apollo Global (APO -4.95%) announced record fee-related earnings, or fee-based operating profit, of $802 million. The asset manager is expanding its private credit infrastructure while shifting investments into higher-quality debt to protect against market volatility. And by scaling its origination network, the firm can capture fee income across market cycles. Three takeaways from the call highlight management's long-term strategy.

High asset valuations and macroeconomic uncertainty led leadership to pull back from lower-rated loans. Instead, management is concentrating capital in senior secured debt and investment-grade assets, which carry credit ratings of BBB or higher. The goal is to preserve principal while still generating reliable yield.

Trading and evaluating private credit has historically suffered from slow pricing systems and limited market liquidity. To fix that, management is spending heavily on new technology to establish daily valuations, standard tracking identifiers, and automated trading platforms for alternative assets.

Financing for artificial intelligence, data centers, and power grid expansions requires massive long-term capital commitments. Apollo Global avoids taking unhedged equity risk in tech. Instead, the firm structures fully amortizing, debt-like loans backed by high-grade corporate guarantees.

Origination volume reached $114 billion in the quarter, with expanding demand across power and compute sectors. Scale, flexible capital, and proprietary origination all support long-term growth as borrowers increasingly seek private solutions over public markets.

And management believes the firm already has everything it needs in-house to deliver on its strategic targets while opening new distribution channels.

#3099. These 4 Restaurant Giants Have Different Ways to Win Diners

Cheap eats, menu buzz, table service, or fresh paint? Here's which restaurant strategy is winning diners right now.

McDonald's (MCD -0.98%), Yum! Brands (YUM -0.37%), Darden Restaurants (DRI -1.54%), and Restaurant Brands International (QSR -0.44%) are all chasing the same customer. That's the person staring at a gas receipt and wondering whether dinner out still makes sense.

Each company has its own way of making the case. McDonald's goes cheap and everywhere. Yum keeps the menu fresh and a little weird. Darden takes care of you at the table. Restaurant Brands is fixing up its restaurants and getting back to basics.

Here's how each pitch is landing in November 2026.

McDonald's sells entry-level food at a scale no rival can match, with more than 45,000 locations worldwide. Its traffic strategy starts with price. The U.S. menu offers $5 Meal Deals, Extra Value Meals, and a $4 breakfast deal. CEO Chris Kempczinski says McDonald's base prices for beef, chicken, and drinks now undercut those of its closest rivals. Management has vowed not to get beaten on value.

The spring push didn't exactly go as planned, though. McDonald's rolled out 10 items for under $3, but about a third of U.S. restaurants didn't price them as recommended, and the launch didn't get much attention. At the same time, the app deals regulars loved went away. U.S. comparable sales rose just 0.8% in the second quarter, and fewer people actually came through the door. Ouch.

Kempczinski called it a bad trade, and the fix is mostly to undo it. The company is restoring digital offers and shifting marketing toward proven value bundles. Call it McBusiness 101.

Yum recently sold Pizza Hut, leaving KFC, Taco Bell, and Habit Burger & Grill in the brand portfolio. The common thread is novelty, and Taco Bell is the poster child.

In the third quarter, it brought back retro favorites through its Decades Menu and teamed up with music artist Peso Pluma and seasoning brand Tajín. It is now launching a pink version of its Baja Blast drink with pop star Olivia Rodrigo. Its Live Más Café test stores have produced more than a dozen new beverages that later rolled out chainwide.

KFC is borrowing its sibling's playbook. Overseas, it's pairing value menus with limited-time items like Captain Nacho. In the U.S., its new Popcorn Chicken sold out in a bunch of restaurants.

Novelty didn't save Taco Bell from a rough summer, though. An industrywide cyclospora outbreak in July knocked U.S. same-store sales down 4% in the third quarter. The menu buzz is helping it climb back, with same-store sales up about 3% over the four weeks ending Oct. 30. That's a pretty quick bounce-back from a serious food safety scare.

Darden is the only full-service operator on my list, and that's the whole pitch. At Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, Yard House, and Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen, someone takes your order, refills your drink, and keeps the food coming. You don't get that service at Mickey D's or Taco Bell. Guest satisfaction scores were at or near record highs last quarter, and a YouGov survey this year ranked Olive Garden No. 1 among casual-dining chains.

"Olive Garden also ranked #1 among Casual Dining brands for service, dining experience and value," CEO Rick Cardenas said on the Q1 2027 earnings call.

And the food really does keep coming. Unlimited soup, salad, and breadsticks are an Olive Garden staple, and this year's Never-Ending Pasta Bowl came with 10,000 Pasta Passes. About 3 million devices logged in to try to snag one, and they sold out immediately. Darden also keeps its price hikes gentle, trailing overall inflation by about 3 percentage points over seven years.

Same-restaurant sales rose 3.2% last quarter. Olive Garden managed just 1%, partly thanks to the World Cup and lettuce worries, but LongHorn grew 6.8% for its 22nd straight positive quarter. My favorite stat: LongHorn spends less than 0.4% of sales on marketing. Good service sells itself.

Restaurant Brands owns Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes, and Firehouse Subs, and its big idea is refreshingly simple. Instead of inventing new stuff, let's try to make the old stuff better.

At Burger King, that starts with the buildings these days. Restaurants remodeled with the new Sizzle design bring in about $2.2 million a year, compared with roughly $1.7 million to $1.8 million for the average location. The remodels are making a difference, and about 40% of the chain still hasn't been updated.

Then there's the menu. Burger King reworked the Whopper and its chicken nuggets instead of chasing trends, and diners noticed. Whopper sales grew by double-digit percentages, and nugget sales soared more than 35%.

As a result, Burger King U.S. comparable sales jumped 8.4% last quarter, nearly 10 points ahead of other burger chains. It's back in the No. 2 spot in the U.S. burger business, trailing only the Golden Arches. Popeyes is trying the same back-to-basics move by trimming wings to focus on its classic fried chicken, but it isn't working yet. U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%.

Right now, the chains polishing what people already like are ahead. Burger King's makeover and Darden's table service are delivering, while McDonald's patches up its value menu and Taco Bell rebuilds after a scary summer.

With gas prices up, diners need a real reason to pull into the parking lot, and some of these companies are giving them a better one than others. Investors need to check up on margins, sales growth, and franchising strategies too, but Darden and Restaurant Brands look like good spots for further research.

If that analysis involves a few lunch orders, I'm sure these companies won't mind the extra business.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased again today, giving buyers modest relief from rates above 7%.

Mortgage rates are continuing to cool off as we head into November.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.93% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3094. Is Google's New Cryptocurrency Service a Reason to Buy Ethereum or Solana?

The company's new platform plays to institutional cybersecurity concerns.

There will soon be a new crypto security service offered by Alphabet (GOOGL +0.37%), and it could well provide a mild boost for Ethereum (ETH +1.20%) and Solana (SOL -0.50%). Google's new cryptocurrency platform, which it calls Google Multi-Party Compute (MPC), was announced on Oct. 28, and Alphabet is already using it to secure its own digital assets parked on both of those blockchains. MPC's commercial launch is scheduled for early 2027.

Google argues its relationships with traditional financial institutions will give it an edge in providing cybersecure crypto custody, but how that will help Solana and Ethereum is another matter. Let's analyze the situation.

MPC is only Alphabet's latest bid to compete more in cryptocurrency.

Google now also runs its own blockchain, the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), which Google unveiled in 2025, and which is also aimed at financial institutions and other approved participants.

The technical basis for the new service is splitting a crypto wallet's private key, the secret code that confers control of the wallet, into fragments that are then held on separate computer systems. This makes it much more difficult for an attacker to assemble a complete private key and proceed with the subsequent theft of funds. Google's tool is also supposed to check each incoming transaction against a list of a financial institution's rules, like spending and transfer limits, before allowing the transaction to proceed.

The fit between this product and its target market is already pretty plainly obvious: In a 2026 survey by American Banker, 47% of the surveyed financial institutions cited cybersecurity as a top barrier to their adoption of blockchain tech. That issue is particularly salient at the moment. On Oct. 29, the largest crypto exchange, Binance, was hacked, and the cyberthieves made off with $6.3 billion.

Google plans to support two different transaction signing methods that institutions can use at launch.

One is the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), which Ethereum uses and which is very widely used elsewhere, and the other is Ed25519, which Solana and many other networks use. Importantly, ECDSA also secures Bitcoin, and the ledger behind XRP, so the company's approach doesn't favor any specific chain.

The bullish factor here for Solana and Ethereum is that Alphabet already uses the platform to secure some of its own digital assets on both chains. It's a minor boost at best.

Offering safer storage to institutions won't make anyone want these coins who does not want them already. Big investors already have custodied access through crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and demand there is both volatile and frequently soft. In the first seven trading days of October 2026, Ethereum ETFs experienced $635 million in net outflows, while Solana ETFs saw $24.8 million in net outflows.

Furthermore, coinholders gain mainly from new net buying and new network usage. Parked coins in long-term storage are rarely used for transactions, adding little to the network activity backing what makes these cryptocurrencies valuable.

Google's GCUL network will be competing for capital and activity, too. Google is pitching the GCUL as a "credibly neutral" permissioned network that any bank can use for payments and asset tokenization, or transforming the ownership rights of stocks and bonds into tradeable crypto. Every bank that chooses to do its work there is business that Ethereum and Solana don't win, and assets they don't get to have parked on their networks.

Therefore, investors should treat this service launch as a small positive, and as a confidence-building step that could eventually lead to some more institutional capital heading to crypto.

In the first half of 2027, watch both coins' ETF flows, and watch for bank announcements of crypto operations naming Google's service as a collaborator. If net ETF inflows return right as banks are signing on, it means that the asset custody story is giving way to new demand, and the situation will be more bullish than it is now.

Alex Carchidi has positions in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3090. Viking Therapeutics Trades 23% Below Its Own $35 Secondary Offering Price. Here's Why That Could Be a Gift for Patient Investors.

Viking aims to enter the weight loss drug market.

Viking Therapeutics (VKTX -2.76%) has been a company to watch over the past few years. That's because the biotech is involved in one of the healthcare market's biggest growth areas: weight loss drugs. Viking hasn't yet commercialized a product, but it's nearing the finish line. The company's lead candidate is involved in two phase 3 trials, and it recently launched trials for an additional candidate.

Viking aims to compete in a space dominated today by pharma giants Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. While I wouldn't expect Viking to oust these players from leadership, the company still could score a major win in the space. This is because demand is high, leaving room for more than one or two companies to operate here.

And today, investors are looking at a key opportunity. Viking is trading about 23% below its $35 secondary offering price. Let's find out why this could be a gift for patient investors.

We'll start by taking a look at the weight loss drug opportunity. The market may reach nearly $100 billion by the end of this decade, analysts predict, and that's due to the tremendous demand for drugs in the GLP-1 class. These products act on hormonal pathways that control digestion, so they help manage blood sugar levels and appetite. Lilly and Novo have generated blockbuster revenue from their injectable GLP-1 drugs, and this year they launched oral products, further broadening the potential patient group.

Viking's VK2735 is being developed in injectable and oral formats. Like Lilly's injectable drugs, Mounjaro and Zepbound, it is a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, so it activates two hormonal pathways involved in digestion. VK2735, as an injectable, is involved in an ongoing phase 3 trial; the oral format recently began its phase 3 study. The company is also studying the candidate in a maintenance dosing trial, with the goal of eventually offering a variety of dosing options to patients.

If all goes smoothly for Viking, it could launch at least one weight loss drug within the next few years. This would be a major moment for the company, ushering in an era of revenue growth.

Meanwhile, Viking also recently started testing another candidate in phase 1, using a different approach. This is an amylin and calcitonin receptor agonist, mimicking the body's hormone amylin and stimulating calcitonin receptors -- both help regulate digestion. This candidate is much further from the finish line, but it's encouraging to see that Viking is filling its pipeline to support potential growth down the road.

The company last month completed a secondary offering, including common stock and convertible senior notes, and raised $575 million to support the phase 3 development of VK 2735. Viking priced the stock at $35, and today, shares are trading about 23% below that level. The stock fell after the operation, as investors frowned on the share dilution that accompanies such an offering. They also didn't like the fact that the offering came at a 16% discount to the previous day's closing price.

Today, however, I'm saying that Viking trading at the current level is a gift to investors. This is because the company is making significant progress in its weight loss pipeline and is nearing the regulatory review stage. If all goes well, Viking could be the next company to join Lilly and Novo in the high-demand weight loss drug space.

In the meantime, clinical trial updates could drive stock performance. Viking stock is known to react to such reports; when it announced phase 2 results for VK2735 a couple of years ago, the stock surged more than 100% in one trading session. That sort of extreme movement may not happen again, but it's likely that positive news still will lead to an increase -- and potential product approval down the road should result in further gains.

Viking's level today, trading at less than $30, seems very reasonable for a biotech at this stage of the development road. All of this means that the stock, trading below its secondary offering level, is a fantastic buy for the patient investor.

Adria Cimino has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Viking Therapeutics. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3084. Tech Sell-Off: 2 Growth Stocks Investors Might Regret Not Buying on the Dip

Artificial intelligence stocks are leading the broader market lower, creating opportunities for investors.

After almost tripling from its 2022 bear market low point, the technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 index is now facing a big test. Investors are increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom, placing pressure on semiconductor stocks like Nvidia and Micron Technology, which are among the largest members of the index.

As a result, the Nasdaq-100 was down 9% from its peak as of the market close last Friday, and the decline could get worse if investor sentiment doesn't improve. However, history suggests this could be a great buying opportunity for investors, because the broader market has always recovered to new highs over the long term.

I'm going to share two stocks investors might regret not buying when they look back on this moment in a few years' time.

Hackers have started using AI to stage highly sophisticated cyber attacks on corporate networks, but enterprises are also placing themselves at risk by exposing their valuable data to third-party AI models without the appropriate guardrails. Zscaler (ZS +0.58%) was one of the early pioneers of the zero trust cybersecurity architecture, which has become one of the best defenses in the AI era.

Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange protects the entire enterprise, starting with the identity layer. It treats every network login attempt as hostile, analyzing the user's credentials, their location, and the device they are using, which maximizes the odds of catching an imposter. Further, the Zero Trust Exchange only allows users to access the applications they need to do their jobs, so even if a hacker bypasses the identity layer, they won't have unrestricted access to the entire network.

Zscaler introduced new tools to the Exchange earlier this year, which protect enterprises when they are deploying AI. There is AI Broker, which constantly monitors communications between AI agents, and Endpoint AI Security, which protects the computers and devices employees are using to run AI software.

Zscaler believes a "Zero Trust Everywhere" approach is the best way to protect against AI threats. Hackers can't attack what they can't see, so keeping critical data, applications, and agents hidden behind the Exchange is the ultimate form of preventative security.

Zscaler had a record year in fiscal 2026 (ended July 31), with revenue growing by 25% to $3.35 billion. Its stock is trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 11.3, so it's already cheaper than competitors like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. Therefore, if a further sell-off in the broader market drags Zscaler stock down with it, investors might be presented with a fantastic long-term buying opportunity.

Meta Platforms (META +2.36%) is the parent company of the Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads social media platforms. Over 3.6 billion people use at least one of them every single day, and considering that is almost half the world's population, it's getting harder for the company to find new signups. As a result, it's trying to lift engagement instead -- if each user spends more time online, they will see more advertisements, and Meta will make more money.

AI is a big part of that strategy. It's embedded in the recommendation algorithms on Facebook and Instagram, where it learns what types of content each user likes to see, and feeds them more of it. According to Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, engagement hit record highs on those apps during the third quarter (ended Sept. 30), so the AI-led strategy appears to be working.

However, there is an even bigger opportunity in the pipeline, and it transcends social media. Meta launched a personal AI agent called Muse in September, and it has already attracted over 10 million users. Zuckerberg recently said one-quarter of them are using it as a personal shopper, with an average purchase value of $200, while others are using it to manage emails, among other things.

Zuckerberg believes Muse could eventually serve billions of people, and it will be capable of improving every area of their lives, whether they want to learn new skills or automate some of life's everyday tasks. This will substantially increase Meta's addressable market, because it could replace the need for traditional internet search engines like Alphabet's Google Search.

Meta stock is down 20% from its peak amid the recent tech sell-off. It's now trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 20.9, so it's much cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 which has a P/E of 29.9. Therefore, this already looks like a good buying opportunity for long-term investors.
